extracted.intended_audience: readers, students of literature, novelists and critics interested in Henry James's views on fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Henry James's critical standards from his essays (especially "The Art of Fiction") about what makes good narrative fiction and the qualities he praised in other writers. Useful for writers and critics seeking James's aesthetic principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Widest possible freedom in content and technique
rubrics_metrics.description: James's argument for the widest possible freedom in content and technique in narrative fiction (from his essay "The Art of Fiction").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The Art of Fiction" argues for the widest possible freedom in content and technique in narrative fiction; writers should not be unduly constrained in choice of subject or method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use imagination beyond personal experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist need not confine themselves to their own experience; imagination and alert observation allow writers to write credibly about matters outside their background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to Walter Besant's recommendation that writers confine themselves to their experience, James argues that 'a sufficiently alert novelist could obtain knowledge from everywhere' and gives the example of a village-born young lady plausibly describing garrison life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary obligation: the novel must be interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: The only precondition James endorses for a novel is that it be interesting; other prescriptive rules are arbitrary by comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'The only obligation to which in advance we may hold a novel, without incurring the accusation of being arbitrary, is that it be interesting.' This is framed as the central evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid restraining fiction with specific moral guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: James is suspicious of rules that restrain fiction on moral grounds or force novels to conform to specific ethical prescriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He warns against treating fiction as a vehicle for imposed moral rules and suggests that art's moral content is covered by depth and seriousness rather than explicit moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of mind; avoid superficiality
rubrics_metrics.description: A good novel should not proceed from a superficial mind; intellectual and artistic depth is required and covers 'all needful moral ground.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'No good novel will ever proceed from a superficial mind; that seems to me an axiom which, for the artist in fiction, will cover all needful moral ground.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers should present a personal, characteristic view
rubrics_metrics.description: Each novelist ought to speak from their own personal perspective; distinct, characteristic accounts of life are valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James's 'house of fiction' image: 'each novelist looks at life from a particular window of the house and thus composes a unique and personally characteristic account.' Encourages varied voices and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigour, precision and conciseness in description
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuing energetic, precise, and concise depiction of life (as James praised in Maupassant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James praised Maupassant's 'vigour, precision and conciseness in describing life as he saw it'—these are presented as desirable qualities in fiction-writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual force
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer's work should exhibit intellectual strength and seriousness (as James praised in George Eliot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James lauded George Eliot for her 'intellectual force,' implying that intellectual rigor and depth are criteria of high fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive, detailed workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Thorough, painstaking detail-work is a virtue in fiction (as James noted in praising Anthony Trollope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as 'stolid but comprehensive detail-work'—attention to concrete detail and sustained craftsmanship are praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unbounded imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Generous imaginative scope and inventiveness are high virtues in fiction (as praised in Robert Louis Stevenson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James admired Stevenson's 'unbounded imagination,' signaling the importance of creative breadth and inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genial common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: A warm, practical sensibility or genial common sense is a positive quality in a writer's work (as James noted of Alphonse Daudet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James praised Daudet's 'genial common sense,' suggesting an appreciation for lucid, commonsensical presentation alongside other virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat narrative fiction as a fine art and take works seriously
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction should be discussed and evaluated as one of the fine arts; critics and readers should take works seriously as important artistic efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that James 'helped to make narrative fiction discussable as one of the fine arts' and that he treated writers' works 'seriously as artistic efforts of the first importance.' This is a meta-criterion for critical approach.
